course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 4
firstTopic.summary: The context for Period 4: a more participatory democracy and a new national culture, an economy transformed by innovation, and a nation that expanded westward and argued over slavery, 1800–1848.

writingQuizzes.title: LEQ: Did economic change create a national identity?

topic.title: African Americans in the Early Republic
topic.summary: How enslaved people resisted and created communities, how free African Americans built institutions and joined antislavery efforts, and what stayed the same and changed in African American life from 1800 to 1848.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes the antislavery efforts of enslaved people in the South between 1800 and 1848?
choices: They led several Southern states to end slavery by law before the Civil War
They won the support of Congress, which banned slavery in the Southern states
They were largely limited to rebellions and plots that did not succeed
They ended when enslaved people were given the right to vote in the Deep South
questions.explanation: Plots and rebellions such as those of Gabriel, Vesey, and Turner were crushed, though enslaved people also resisted in daily ways.
choiceExplanations: No Southern state ended slavery in these years.
Congress did not ban slavery in the Southern states.
Plots and rebellions such as those of Gabriel, Vesey, and Turner were crushed, though enslaved people also resisted in daily ways.
Enslaved people had no voting rights.
questions.distinguisher: The state laws choice is close because Northern states did pass such laws, but Southern states did not.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a result of Nat Turner's rebellion in 1831?
choices: Southern legislatures tightened the slave codes and restricted education and movement
Virginia ended slavery after the rebellion showed that it was dangerous to the state
Congress banned the movement of enslaved people from the Upper South to the Deep South
The rebels won their freedom and founded a settlement in Southampton County
questions.explanation: White Southerners responded to the rebellion with harsher laws, and a debate over ending slavery in Virginia produced no change.
choiceExplanations: White Southerners responded to the rebellion with harsher laws, and a debate over ending slavery in Virginia produced no change.
Virginia did not end slavery.
Congress took no such action.
The rebellion was suppressed.
questions.distinguisher: The Virginia ended slavery choice is close because the legislature debated the issue in 1832, but it did not act.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Denmark Vesey's plot of 1822 in Charleston, South Carolina, was
choices: a successful uprising that freed the enslaved people on the coast of the state
discovered before it began, and the authorities executed its leaders
a rebellion in Virginia, led by Gabriel, that threatened the city of Richmond
a revolt by free Black sailors against the officers of ships in Charleston
questions.explanation: Authorities uncovered the plan and executed Vesey and others, and South Carolina tightened its laws.
choiceExplanations: The plot was discovered before it was carried out.
Authorities uncovered the plan and executed Vesey and others, and South Carolina tightened its laws.
That describes Gabriel's plot of 1800.
The plot aimed to end slavery in the region.
questions.distinguisher: The Gabriel choice is close because both were planned rebellions, but Gabriel's plot was in Virginia in 1800.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Why did enslaved people work to keep family ties across plantations despite the threat of sale?
choices: Slaveholders were required by law to keep enslaved families together
Kin ties were needed to qualify for freedom under the laws of the Southern states
Families wanted to gather enough money to purchase land and to start farms
Family ties protected their dignity and gave them support
questions.explanation: Enslaved people built families and kin networks that gave comfort and cultural continuity, even when the law did not recognize them.
choiceExplanations: The law gave enslaved families no protection.
No such law existed.
Enslaved people had few means to purchase land.
Enslaved people built families and kin networks that gave comfort and cultural continuity, even when the law did not recognize them.
questions.distinguisher: The slaveholder requirement choice is close because some owners kept families together, but the law did not require it.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The African Methodist Episcopal Church, founded by Richard Allen in 1816, was
choices: a missionary society that sent freed people to settle in Liberia
a Black-led denomination that gave free Black people a church of their own
a Southern church that taught enslaved people to obey their enslavers
an abolitionist newspaper that demanded the immediate end of slavery
questions.explanation: Free African Americans built churches, schools, and mutual aid societies that served as centers of community life and activism.
choiceExplanations: That describes the American Colonization Society.
Free African Americans built churches, schools, and mutual aid societies that served as centers of community life and activism.
The AME Church was independent and based in the North.
It was a church and not a newspaper.
questions.distinguisher: The missionary society choice is close because it also concerned Black Americans, but the AME Church was a church.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a continuity in the experience of African Americans from 1800 to 1848?
choices: Most African Americans remained enslaved, and slavery continued to expand in the South
Slavery ended in every state south of Virginia after the Atlantic slave trade closed
Free Black people gained equal political rights in the North and the South
Enslaved families were protected from sale by laws passed by Congress
questions.explanation: The power of slavery and racial prejudice continued even as free Black institutions and abolitionism grew.
choiceExplanations: The power of slavery and racial prejudice continued even as free Black institutions and abolitionism grew.
Slavery spread in the Deep South.
Free Black people faced growing restrictions.
Congress did not protect them.
questions.distinguisher: The ending of slavery choice is close because the importation of enslaved Africans ended in 1808, but slavery itself expanded.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: David Walker's Appeal (1829) is best known for
choices: urging free Black Americans to move to Africa and found a new nation there
defending the gradual end of slavery as a policy that Southerners could support
calling on enslaved people to resist and condemning slavery
arguing that Congress should buy the freedom of the enslaved from their owners
questions.explanation: Walker's pamphlet alarmed Southern leaders and encouraged more militant Black activism.
choiceExplanations: Walker opposed colonization.
Walker demanded resistance and an end to slavery.
Walker's pamphlet alarmed Southern leaders and encouraged more militant Black activism.
He called on Black Americans to resist.
questions.distinguisher: The colonization choice is close because many writers discussed it, but Walker urged resistance.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why free Black Northerners founded their own churches, schools, and mutual aid societies?
choices: State law required Black communities to build all of their own institutions
White institutions excluded them, so they built institutions of their own
White churches and schools had been closed in the North by order of the courts
Free Black people had no interest in education or religion until the 1830s
questions.explanation: Excluded from many white institutions, free Black communities created their own and used them for mutual support and activism.
choiceExplanations: State law did not require it.
Excluded from many white institutions, free Black communities created their own and used them for mutual support and activism.
White institutions remained open.
They had long valued both.
questions.distinguisher: The state law choice is close because segregation was often enforced by law, but communities also built institutions by choice.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The growth of the internal slave trade is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A decline in the demand for cotton that left planters with surplus workers
A federal plan to resettle enslaved people on land in the Northwest Territory
The abolition of slavery in the Upper South by gradual emancipation laws
The expansion of cotton and the end of the Atlantic slave trade in 1808
questions.explanation: With the importation of enslaved Africans banned, planters in the Deep South bought people from the Upper South.
choiceExplanations: Demand for cotton rose.
No such plan was made.
Slavery continued in the Upper South.
With the importation of enslaved Africans banned, planters in the Deep South bought people from the Upper South.
questions.distinguisher: The declining demand choice is close because the Upper South's tobacco economy weakened, but the demand for cotton workers rose.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following claims about Douglass's experience is best supported by the excerpt?
choices: Douglass believed that reading would make slaveholders treat the enslaved with kindness
Douglass learned to read because his master encouraged him to seek an education
Reading gave Douglass an understanding of slavery and a path to freedom
Douglass had always known how slavery worked and did not need to learn it
questions.explanation: Douglass says that he understood “the pathway from slavery to freedom” once he understood the white man's power to enslave.
choiceExplanations: He describes understanding the power of the white man over the black man.
The excerpt refers to his master's objections.
Douglass says that he understood “the pathway from slavery to freedom” once he understood the white man's power to enslave.
He describes it as a new revelation.
questions.distinguisher: The kindness choice is close because the excerpt is about learning, but Douglass drew a lesson about power and freedom.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.12, KC-4.1.II.D: enslaved and free African Americans created strategies to protect their dignity and joined efforts aimed at changing their status
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Frederick Douglass, who escaped from slavery in 1838, writing about his time as an enslaved boy in Baltimore, in his Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave, published in 1845
stimulusBlocks.citation: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (Boston, 1845), chap. 6. Project Gutenberg eBook #23.
stimulusBlocks.note: “These words” are the objections of Hugh Auld, Douglass’s master in Baltimore, to his wife Sophia Auld teaching the young Douglass to read.
stimulusBlocks.text: These words sank deep into my heart, stirred up sentiments within that lay slumbering, and called into existence an entirely new train of thought. It was a new and special revelation, explaining dark and mysterious things, with which my youthful understanding had struggled, but struggled in vain. I now understood what had been to me a most perplexing difficulty--to wit, the white man's power to enslave the black man. It was a grand achievement, and I prized it highly. From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom. It was just what I wanted, and I got it at a time when I the least expected it.

questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a claim and/or argument in a text-based or non-text-based source.

questions.prompt: Douglass most likely wrote the Narrative (1845) in order to
choices: persuade Northern readers that slavery was wrong
provide a legal brief for a lawsuit seeking the freedom of his family from their owners
defend the slaveholders who had taught him to read from the charges of cruelty
urge Congress to pay slaveholders for the freedom of enslaved people
questions.explanation: Douglass was a leading abolitionist, and his narrative gave Northern readers a firsthand account of the injustice of slavery.
choiceExplanations: Douglass was a leading abolitionist, and his narrative gave Northern readers a firsthand account of the injustice of slavery.
It was a published autobiography and not a legal brief.
He wrote to condemn slavery.
The Narrative argued against slavery and did not seek compensation.
questions.distinguisher: The legal brief choice is close because Douglass later sought legal rights, but the Narrative was written for a public audience.

questions.prompt: The words that “sank deep” into Douglass's heart most directly led him to
choices: give up his efforts to learn to read in order to avoid trouble
see literacy as a pathway to freedom and to seek to learn despite the risks
ask his master to free him in return for his labor and his loyalty
join a Northern abolitionist society at once and publish a newspaper
questions.explanation: Hugh Auld's objections taught Douglass that knowledge made slavery impossible to keep, and he determined to learn.
choiceExplanations: He describes the words as a revelation that he prized.
Hugh Auld's objections taught Douglass that knowledge made slavery impossible to keep, and he determined to learn.
The excerpt does not say that he asked for freedom.
That came later in his life.
questions.distinguisher: The give-up choice is close because the words were a warning, but Douglass drew the opposite lesson.
